name: Breadboard

claims.claim_text: Breakout boards that convert surface-mount packages into DIP footprints exist because parts still need to plug into breadboards, and they are cheap and simple to fabricate.
claims.quote_verbatim: Yeah, well, you've always got to plug into breadboards. So those sort of breakout boards where you convert surface mount into dip packages, they're, you know, easy and cheap to do.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Transistor Types and Where To Get Electronic Gear

claims.claim_text: A full panel of mixed-footprint adapter boards cost roughly twenty to thirty dollars, cheap enough to keep on hand so any chip can be made breadboard-ready.
claims.quote_verbatim: Yeah, you can buy one of these panels for, you know, $20, $30 or something.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Transistor Types and Where To Get Electronic Gear

claims.claim_text: When a build technique is laborious enough that a mistake costs another hour or two of rework, breadboarding the circuit instead is the more sensible route.
claims.quote_verbatim: If I'm going to do that, I may as well build the circuit up on breadboard or something, you know?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Callow Cough Coverups

claims.claim_text: Soldering gold 0.1-inch-spaced conversion headers onto an SD card lets the card plug straight into a breadboard so its pins can be broken out for experimentation.
claims.quote_verbatim: They actually soldered some... Like, some gold 100 mil spaced headers. Like, conversion headers. To a SD card. And then they plugged that directly into a breadboard. So, you could just break out the pins.
claims.episode_title: Op amps, Microchips & Mergers - Narquois Nerd Nescience - Narquois Nerd Nescience

claims.claim_text: Forcing a large square 0.1-inch header into a breadboard spreads the internal spring contacts permanently apart, ruining the tie point for later use with normal-sized leads.
claims.quote_verbatim: the spring contacts inside, it pushes them apart and it forces them apart. You know, if you try and push a big square, 0.1-inch header into the breadboard, it's not designed for that.
claims.episode_title: Op amps, Microchips & Mergers - Narquois Nerd Nescience - Narquois Nerd Nescience

claims.claim_text: Tiny breadboards bought in bulk make a no-soldering-iron entry point for demonstrating circuits to children.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't need a soldering iron because you can just throw in, like, a little tiny breadboard or something. They're cheap. If you bought them in bulk from eBay or something
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard successors, CAD & Robots - Haussmannized Halloween Hypostrophe

claims.claim_text: A common bench rule of thumb puts the usable upper frequency limit of a solderless breadboard at about 10 MHz.
claims.quote_verbatim: Ah, yeah, you would rule of thumb breadboard stops at about 10.
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: A microcontroller with a 50 MHz internal clock can still be breadboarded, because the internal core speed is not what appears on the pins; only signals actually toggling on the wiring face the breadboard's frequency limit.
claims.quote_verbatim: you certainly can, can operate higher because it's only internally operating at that. It, it, it isn't like you're trying to, you know, drive, you know, it's not like trying to toggle the output pins at 50 megahertz.
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: Once parts arrive in 0.5 mm pitch surface-mount packages, breadboarding requires ordering breakout boards you probably do not stock, at which point ordering a fabricated PCB costs about the same wait.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, yeah, you can get breakout boards, but I don't keep those in stock, you know? I've got to, oh, I might as well, you know, by the time I order that, I might as well order a board, you know?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: High-speed data converter work, on the order of 20 mega-samples per second, cannot be evaluated on a breadboard because the wiring parasitics corrupt the measurement.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I'm doing 20 mega samples, I'm not doing 20 mega samples on a frigging, you know, breadboard because, you know, those kind of, you'll start getting parasitics in there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: Writing a project-based electronics book meant physically building and testing roughly 26 separate breadboards, close to one per chapter, to confirm every circuit actually worked.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have roughly about 20, roughly about 26 breadboards. It came out. Wow. Almost one breadboard per chapter.
claims.speaker: Ron Quan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ron Quan - Tenacious Transistor Teacher

claims.claim_text: An augmented-reality assembly aid can use a small printed tracker sticker placed on the breadboard so a phone camera can register the board and overlay graphics showing where each wire goes.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have a small tracker sticker on the breadboard and you hold your phone up to it and it basically overlays it two to be graphic showing you where the, the lines are
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: For a breadboard-oriented learning product the hardware is the commodity part; the differentiating work is the libraries and a guided multi-circuit course that walks a beginner through wiring each part.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've built a course that guides people on either their iPad or their Microsoft Surface or even in Chrome how to build 11 different circuits
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: A high-efficiency power conversion design competition is out of reach of breadboard prototyping; efficiency targets in that range demand real layout from the start.
claims.quote_verbatim: you won't prototype this on a breadboard right don't even think about it right it's just not going to happen right
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: Wiring a bare microcontroller yourself on a breadboard, including its crystal and decoupling, surfaces the problems a prebuilt development platform hides, which is why it is worth doing at least once.
claims.quote_verbatim: Just put it on a breadboard, put your crystal, put your decoupling, put your – and just find out how many problems you're going to run into.
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: One teaching approach presents a virtual breadboard inside a game world that the learner must then reproduce with real parts, using the game as the motivation to build the physical circuit.
claims.quote_verbatim: the idea is that you see the breadboard in Minecraft world, but you have to replicate it in the real world
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: Through-hole resistors pulled off bandolier tape carry glue residue on the leads; pushed straight into a breadboard that residue can prevent contact or act like a small series capacitance, so the leads should be trimmed first.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you take that resistor and then go stick it straight in your breadboard, congratulations. You've got a layer of bloody glue on your pin. And it may not make contact.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: Even a modest breadboard build consumes surprising amounts of time, because each part has to be fetched from the drawer, measured, and its leads prepared before insertion.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not a huge breadboard layout, but it took time. You know? I was surprised how long it took.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: Modern chips shipped in surface-mount packages with formed gull-wing leads physically cannot be inserted into a breadboard without an adapter.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't even plug these chips into a breadboard because they're all bloody desold and all the legs are bent
claims.episode_title: Robots are coming - Ominous Operational Overhaul

claims.claim_text: A whole ARM Cortex-M0 plus a 2.4 GHz Bluetooth Low Energy radio can be packaged on a tiny module shaped as a 16-pin DIP so it drops into a breadboard like an ordinary through-hole chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's basically a 16-pin dip, 2, 4, 6, 8, yep, 16-pin dip package, tiny little board. So it fits in your breadboard as a regular dip chip.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Part Choice Triathlon

claims.claim_text: Breadboards with long hanging jumper wires add capacitance and act as an antenna, which is particularly hostile to an open-drain I2C bus and pushes you toward lower pull-up values.
claims.quote_verbatim: When you've got things, when you've got breadboards and wires hanging everywhere, you've got capacitance and you've got a big antenna, basically. And when you've got an I-squared C, that is not ideal for an I-squared C line.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Our First Call In Show

claims.claim_text: SPI is more robust than I2C on messy prototype wiring because its totem-pole outputs drive both logic levels directly and need no pull-up resistors.
claims.quote_verbatim: You don't need a pull-up resistor on a SPI line because it's just driving directly.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Our First Call In Show

claims.claim_text: Migrating a working breadboard circuit onto soldered perf board is a deliberate learning exercise: the mistakes it forces are cheap to fix with solder and wire, and troubleshooting them is where the skill is built.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is inherent value in taking a circuit that you have on a breadboard
claims.episode_title: Eating An Elephant

claims.claim_text: When a product's entire challenge is its final mechanical form factor and the electronics are a microcontroller with known-good sensors, breadboard prototyping adds nothing and the first prototype should be the final design.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's no point prototyping it on a breadboard or a variaboard or whatever because, like, it's just a micro with some capacitive touch sensors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Artificially Intelligent Party Platform

claims.claim_text: A high pin-count part with no through-hole option forces you past breadboarding straight into committing to a six or eight layer board simply to fan out its signals.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't just breadboard this thing, right? And like, you know, you've got to commit. Do you have a dip package, please? You've got to commit to like, what, a six or eight layer board or something to fan out all the stuff.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Breadboards leave every conductor exposed, which becomes a genuine shock hazard when a high voltage supply is being switched on and off during a test.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm turning the high voltage supply off and on and all these exposed wirings on the breadboard and everything else
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Magical Fire Bags

claims.claim_text: Buying an interesting part in a 24-pin QFN package commits you to building a DIP breakout for it before any breadboard experimentation is possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just bought the ones that came in 24-pin QFN packages. So it's like, well, if I want to use this on a breadboard, I got to dipify it.
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Paper-and-copper-tape circuits suit expressive, drawing-based teaching in a way breadboards do not, because a breadboard is awkward and clumsy as a medium for annotating and telling a story around a circuit.
claims.quote_verbatim: Whereas if you're in a breadboard and you want to do any sort of stuff, it's a little awkward and clumsy for that.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: The intermediate polished one-off build stage can be skipped entirely: once a breadboard or veroboard proof of concept works, go straight to the production PCB.
claims.quote_verbatim: The proof of concept is you've already breadboarded or veriborded the thing. Right. Like, so, that's it. I'd jump from that straight to the production PCB.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Total 360

claims.claim_text: A shipping robotics product can begin as an Arduino, a shield, a mini breadboard and a handful of jumper wires; breadboard-level construction is not automatically disqualifying for a first commercial unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: the circuit board was literally an Arduino and then a shield and then a, uh, one of those little mini breadboards and like six wires to connect up
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Breadboard wiring stays workable up to roughly 10 MHz, below which layout parasitics generally do not need close attention.
claims.quote_verbatim: up until like about 10 megahertz or so, you don't really have to worry too much
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pedantic or Andrantic

claims.claim_text: Strong prototypers extract the most from whatever hardware is already at hand, whether that means wire wrap, bodging development boards together, or a breadboard, rather than jumping immediately into PCB layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: the best prototypers, I think they take what they can, they do the most they can with the hardware they have
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pedantic or Andrantic

claims.claim_text: Building a computer on breadboards keeps the machine visually legible for teaching, whereas a schematic turned into a fabricated PCB hides the operation behind a finished assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it felt a little bit to me anyway, kind of sort of removed. If you, you know, draw a schematic in a CAD package and then you spit out a PCB and you send it off and it gets manufactured and you just solder it up and it works.
claims.speaker: Ben Eater
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Eater

claims.claim_text: A breadboard teaching kit should ship high quality breadboards and enough current limiting resistors for every LED, because component quality directly changes the learner's odds of getting a working circuit.
claims.quote_verbatim: It comes with a very high quality breadboards. So I try to include everything that optimize your, your likelihood for success. It also comes with enough current limiting resistors that you can put resistors on all the LEDs.
claims.speaker: Ben Eater
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Eater

claims.claim_text: A large breadboard build involves so much cutting, stripping and bending of wire that a mistake is effectively guaranteed, which makes troubleshooting an unavoidable and valuable part of the exercise.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's complex enough that you're basically guaranteed to make a mistake somewhere along the way, which means that you're guaranteed to have to do some amount of troubleshooting
claims.speaker: Ben Eater
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Eater

claims.claim_text: Milling a custom breakout board for every component used, fanning even sub-millimeter-pitch BGAs out to 2.5 mm pins, keeps otherwise unusable parts available for breadboard work.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically every component I ended up using, uh, I create a breakout board for it. Uh-huh. It breaks out to 2.5 millimeter pins
claims.speaker: Mike Grover
claims.episode_title: An Interview with MG (Mike Grover)

claims.claim_text: A DIP package is itself a breakout: a tiny die is bonded out to a comparatively huge lead frame, so a home-made adapter board is doing structurally the same job as the packaging house.
claims.quote_verbatim: even when you buy a dip part these days, it's effectively the same thing. Just internally, they're bonding out the chip, the tiny, tiny bit of silicon up to these huge lead frames.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with MG (Mike Grover)

claims.claim_text: A classic breadboarded TTL logic exercise failed for an entire class because of a fan-out violation, with one gate driving around a dozen inputs beyond its drive strength.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was a fan out problem. We had what, like one gate driving like, you know, 12 others.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: A signal leaving a die in a DIP part traverses a bond wire, the lead frame leg, the breadboard's spring clip and then a jumper wire, and each of those transitions is a parasitic discontinuity that on-die interconnect avoids entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're going through a dip package to a, through a breadboard, through a jumper wire, my God, like the fact that it works at all, when you start to look at it like that is really amazing.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The usual project order is breadboard the circuit, write code, then build the real circuit and enclosure; inverting it to enclosure first, then electronics, then code, guarantees something presentable exists if the project stalls partway.
claims.quote_verbatim: I start with the enclosure, then add the electronics, then add the code.
claims.speaker: Zack Freedman
claims.episode_title: Finishing Prototypes with Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: Breadboarding is perfectly adequate provided the restrictions are understood; slow loads such as relays present no problem for the medium.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mean, I have breadboarding. It gets the job done sometimes. Yeah. As long as people know the, uh, the restrictions, you know, like relays, slow stuff, no big deal.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Feed the Mouse

claims.claim_text: A chunky 10 A 240 V relay can sit on a breadboard for control-side work, but mains voltage must not be run through breadboard contacts.
claims.quote_verbatim: Everyone thought I was going to be putting mains through it. It's like, no, you can't put mains on breadboard.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Feed the Mouse

claims.claim_text: A breadboard test setup is not repeatable, because a single wire shifting changes the result and adds an uncontrolled variable to any measurement.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's just like a breadboard is for testing. It's fine. And then a wire moves and yeah, it's just not, it's not repeatable.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: For audio-band work such as trying out different filter topologies, a breadboard is hard to beat as a prototyping medium.
claims.quote_verbatim: for audio, like if you're just trying to, you know, design different filters or anything like that breadboard, you can't beat that
claims.speaker: Philip Salmony
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: Mechanical environments such as a quadcopter or fixed-wing aircraft rule out breadboard construction because vibration will shake the friction-fit connections loose, forcing the move to a soldered circuit board.
claims.quote_verbatim: just talking about like vibration on a quadcopter or a, you know, fixed wing. It's like, yeah, that, that, that breadboard is not going to work.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: Intermittent debug-port failures traced with a logic analyzer turned out to be noise injected by a makeshift breadboard test setup rather than a fault in the design under test.
claims.quote_verbatim: find some, uh, noise coming on my line from my perhaps a little bit janky breadboard setup
claims.speaker: Laura Abbott
claims.episode_title: Finding Hardware Flaws with Laura Abbott

claims.claim_text: A workable project rule for group builds is to allow breadboards but cap the design at twenty jumper wires, since the wire count is what makes a build unmanageable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't have more than 20 jumper wires. So if the project takes more than 20, it's not.
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Rebuilding Projects with Dave Young

claims.claim_text: The term breadboard is literal in origin: early experimenters used a wooden bread-cutting board with nails or small ceramic-based terminals hammered into it as tie points.
claims.quote_verbatim: the term breadboard came from that space, right? Where it was actually like a piece of wood people were cutting bread on and then they hammered nails into it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Open Circuits with Eric Schlaepfer and Windell Oskay

claims.claim_text: Connecting an unpackaged board's red and black power leads directly to a 120 V mains outlet destroys it immediately, a first-hand demonstration that a low-voltage supply input is not a mains input.
claims.quote_verbatim: I plugged the red wire and the black wire into the 120 volt outlet and smoke came out.
claims.speaker: Don Wilcher
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: Graduating with complete paper knowledge of a classic op-amp such as the 741 leaves you unable to wire it on a breadboard and power it up, which is why bench practice has to accompany theory.
claims.quote_verbatim: I wouldn't have, you know, probably idea on how to put it on a breadboard and power it up and use it for doing something
claims.speaker: Andrea Longobardi
claims.episode_title: Low Power Connected Devices with Andrea Longobardi

claims.claim_text: The jumperless breadboard places an LED behind every row so individual channels light up to show connectivity.
claims.quote_verbatim: So like it's backlit, right? It's backlit. There is a lead behind every row on the breadboard. It lights up individual channels.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Really long needle nose pliers

claims.claim_text: A castellated microcontroller module can serve simultaneously as a solderable module, a reference design and a dev board, with header-fitted variants produced specifically so it drops into a breadboard alongside a debug connector.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'd like to produce these headed versions where you can easily put them into a breadboard and plug in the, uh, the debug, um, with a connector
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A jumperless breadboard replaces the wires with analog crossbar switch chips, the same class of part historically used for audio mixers and video switching matrices.
claims.quote_verbatim: No, it's the same circuit, like same chips, analog crossbar switches.
claims.speaker: Kevin Cappuccio
claims.episode_title: A Jumperless Breadboard with Kevin Cappuccio

claims.claim_text: A standard breadboard is a poor design from a signal integrity standpoint, and its convenience is the sole reason it survives on benches.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is a terrible design. And signal integrity wise, it's a bad idea, but it's, boy, is it convenient.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Jumperless Breadboard with Kevin Cappuccio

claims.claim_text: The crossbar switches used in a jumperless breadboard are rated to about 50 MHz, comfortably above the frequency the breadboard's own mechanical contacts can support, so the switches are not the bandwidth bottleneck.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's 50 megahertz is like what they're kind of rated for. Like the switches. Yeah. Um, which is well above what a breadboard physically can handle.
claims.speaker: Kevin Cappuccio
claims.episode_title: A Jumperless Breadboard with Kevin Cappuccio

claims.claim_text: The impedance discontinuity at the junction between a component's resistor leg and the breadboard's spring clip is already enough to degrade high-frequency signals before any other parasitic is considered.
claims.quote_verbatim: I guess probably just the, uh, resistor leg to, uh, tulip connection. Probably you've already have some discontinuity enough there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Jumperless Breadboard with Kevin Cappuccio

claims.claim_text: The classic breadboard failure is a wire not fully seated in its hole: the circuit does not work until something jostles the wire deeper into the contact, costing hours of lab time.
claims.quote_verbatim: the circuit isn't working. And then they kind of like tap the top of the wires and then one wire kind of finds its way further into the hole
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Jumperless Breadboard with Kevin Cappuccio

claims.claim_text: Inside a breadboard each row of five holes shares one bent metal clip, and in the jumperless design that clip is soldered down to the PCB through two solder joints at its ends, forming a single net.
claims.quote_verbatim: So those are soldered down. So all five of those holes go to those two solder joints at the top and bottom.
claims.speaker: Kevin Cappuccio
claims.episode_title: A Jumperless Breadboard with Kevin Cappuccio

claims.claim_text: For small-run silicon the packaging cost matches the silicon cost, roughly seven dollars each, whereas chip-on-board packaging can bring the packaging portion under two dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: silicon is seven bucks, but it costs you seven more dollars to do the packaging of the chip
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: A chip-on-board PCB carrying a bare die can be shaped to present DIP pins, giving a breadboard-compatible part and letting new silicon drop into legacy through-hole designs such as Z80 sockets.
claims.quote_verbatim: it could be a breadboard compatible, you know, dip pin chip
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

attribution_notes: Passage [41] (ep 369) and [75] (ep 703) are flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE. For ep 369 the speaker label says Jason Huggins and the content matches him describing his own robot company and his fondness for Fritzing, so the label was kept. For ep 703 the label says Tim Ansell and the content is the wafer.space founder describing his own packaging economics, so the label was kept.

Ep 62 passages [5]/[6]/[7] overlap on the same dialogue and the labels flip between Dave Jones and Chris Gammell across the shared text. The spring-contact / oversized-pin explanation is attributed null because the label alternates on identical text.

Ep 68 passages [9] and [10] carry the same dialogue with opposite labels. The '10 MHz rule of thumb' is the answer to the question about 50 MHz limitations; the answering voice is the more senior bench practitioner (Dave Jones) but the labels conflict, so it is attributed null.

Ep 110 passage [12] is labeled Chris Gammell; the speaker refers to starting Chip Report TV and then asks the other person about 'your USB power supply', which identifies the other person as Dave Jones. The parasitics/20-mega-samples claims are therefore given to Chris Gammell, and the reply about reusing an old board as an SPI/I2C driving platform is given to Dave Jones.
Ep 133 header lists guest 'Ron Kwan' and speaker 'Ron Quan' (same person, transcription variant). Attributed as Ron Quan.

Ep 110 passage [12] is labeled Chris Gammell; the speaker refers to starting Chip Report TV and then asks the other person about 'your USB power supply', which identifies the other person as Dave Jones, so the parasitics and breakout-board claims are attributed to Chris Gammell.

Ep 360 passage [40] is labeled Dave Jones; the content ('See, I wouldn't do the one-off build') is the responder to Chris Gammell's project-stage map, consistent with Dave Jones, so the label was kept.

Ep 454 passage [47]/[48]: the breakout-board-per-component content is Mike Grover describing his own mill workflow; the follow-on remark about DIP parts being bonded to large lead frames is the interviewer's, so it is attributed null.

Ep 689 passages are labeled inconsistently between Chris Gammell and Kevin Cappuccio across overlapping text. Statements describing the jumperless hardware's own design decisions (crossbar chips, custom clips with holes, solder joints, connection feedback) are attributed to Kevin Cappuccio; the general breadboard commentary and the walk-through questions are attributed to Chris Gammell or null where the overlap makes it unclear.

Ep 689 passages are labeled inconsistently between Chris Gammell and Kevin Cappuccio across overlapping text. Statements describing the jumperless hardware's own design decisions (crossbar chips, solder joints, switch ratings) are attributed to Kevin Cappuccio; general breadboard commentary and walk-through questions are attributed to Chris Gammell.
